title: What is the difference between batch and stream processing engines (e.g. Spark batch vs Spark Structured Streaming / Flink), and when do you use micro-batch vs true record-at-a-time streaming?
shortTitle: Batch vs stream processing engines, and micro-batch vs record-at-a-time
keyPoints: Spark batch processes a bounded dataset in scheduled runs, optimizing for throughput with Catalyst and Tungsten.
Spark Structured Streaming uses micro-batch: tiny bounded batches triggered at short intervals, reusing Spark's optimizer.
Flink uses true record-at-a-time: each event flows through operators individually for lowest latency.
Micro-batch has a latency floor equal to the trigger interval (hundreds of milliseconds to seconds).
Record-at-a-time can achieve low-millisecond latency with precise event-time handling and rich keyed state.
Use batch for nightly reports; micro-batch for near-real-time dashboards; Flink for fraud blocking under tight latency.
The line has blurred: Spark added continuous mode, Flink supports batch over bounded streams.

s1_definition.oneliner: Batch processes finished chunks on a schedule, micro-batch processes tiny continuous stacks with a small latency floor, and record-at-a-time processes each event instantly for the lowest latency.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Batch engine** – processes a bounded dataset in scheduled runs, optimizing for throughput and cost (e.g., Spark batch).
- **Micro-batch** – streaming that groups events into tiny bounded batches processed at short intervals, giving high throughput with a small latency floor (e.g., Spark Structured Streaming).
- **Record-at-a-time** – streaming that processes each event individually as it arrives, giving the lowest latency and finer-grained state (e.g., Apache Flink).
- **Trigger interval** – the micro-batch frequency; the latency floor of Structured Streaming.
- **Checkpoint barriers** – markers Flink injects into the stream to snapshot state for exactly-once fault tolerance.
- **Catalyst optimizer** – Spark's query planner that micro-batch reuses from batch, a key operational advantage.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India can total transactions three ways. A batch engine is the night shift totalling the whole day's pile at once. Spark Structured Streaming's micro-batch is like a clerk who scoops up whatever slips landed in the last half-second and processes that little scoop, then the next scoop: continuous but in tiny stacks. Flink's record-at-a-time is a clerk who processes each slip the exact instant it touches the counter, never waiting to form a stack. Night-shift batch is cheapest for big reports; scoops are a great balance for most streaming; and per-slip is the choice when every millisecond counts, like blocking a fraudulent swipe instantly.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Three Processing Models
  ───────────────────────

  Spark Batch (bounded, scheduled)
  [Day's data] ──▶ [Optimize] ──▶ [Run all] ──▶ [Result] ──▶ STOP

  Spark Structured Streaming (micro-batch)
  [Events] ──▶ [Scoop 0.5s] ──▶ [Process] ──▶ [Scoop] ──▶ [Process] ──▶ ...
              └─ trigger ─┘    └─ result ─┘

  Flink (record-at-a-time)
  [Event] ──▶ [Process] ──▶ [Event] ──▶ [Process] ──▶ [Event] ──▶ ...
  (each event processed individually, ms latency)
```

```text
  Latency Spectrum
  ────────────────
  Batch         Micro-Batch       Record-at-a-Time
  (hours)       (seconds)         (milliseconds)
  ◄────────────────────────────────────────────────►
  Spark Batch   Spark Streaming   Flink
  Cheapest      Good balance      Lowest latency
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A batch engine like Spark batch processes a bounded dataset in scheduled runs, reading the whole chunk, building an optimized plan, running it, and stopping. This makes it efficient for large joins and aggregations and ideal for end-of-day reports and backfills. Spark Structured Streaming uses micro-batch, treating the stream as tiny bounded batches triggered every short interval, reusing Spark's Catalyst optimizer and DataFrame API for high throughput with a latency floor of roughly the trigger interval. Flink uses true record-at-a-time processing, flowing each event through operators individually for low-millisecond latency, with precise event-time handling and exactly-once via checkpoint barriers.

Choosing between them comes down to latency, throughput, state complexity, and operational simplicity. Use batch when freshness is not critical and cost wins. Use micro-batch when near-real-time of a second or two is good enough and you value one unified API. Use record-at-a-time when you need the lowest latency, sophisticated per-event stateful logic, or the strongest event-time semantics.

The line has blurred, since Spark added continuous mode and Flink supports batch over bounded streams, so the real decision is your latency budget, how complex your state is, and which engine your team already operates well.

In a banking context at the National Bank of India, nightly reports ran on Spark batch, near-real-time dashboards ran on Spark Structured Streaming, and the latency-critical fraud jobs ran on Flink where processing each swipe instantly let the bank block a fraudulent transaction immediately. Matching the engine to the workload is what kept the platform cost-effective and fast where it mattered.

Remember one sentence: batch for throughput, micro-batch for near-real-time balance, record-at-a-time for lowest latency, and match the engine to the workload.
